claims.notes: THE TOWN'S TWO RIVER BRIDGES, DIMENSIONED, AND THEY ALREADY STAND. This is the single most useful thing February 1834 says to a reconstruction. The Trustees of the Town of Chicago advertise for proposals to REPAIR — not to build — the bridges over the North and South branches of the Chicago river, and the specification is a parts list: braces of oak timber 6 inches square, a new bent to one bridge, two complete sets of braces for each, oak railing 8 by 4 inches for both, oak standards for the railing 4 feet high, flooring of oak plank 2 inches thick, the flooring pinned down with oak pins 1 1-2 inches in diameter and 2 feet long, the railing secured by spikes or pins. EVERY ONE OF THOSE IS A MODELLABLE DIMENSION and they are the town's own words, not a retrospective plate's. What is NOT here is span, width or height, and none of it is supplied — the notice describes what is to be renewed, not the whole structure. The date matters as much as the timber: both branch bridges exist and are in need of repair in January 1834, eighteen months before the scene date, so a reconstruction that shows them standing in 1835 is standing on a documented floor rather than on an assumption. G. W. Dole and John Miller sign for the Trustees. The column is a Tesseract fallback and its left edge is cut, so the bracketed supplies are the recurring formulae of a proposals notice; the dimensions themselves are all read off the line uncut.

claims.notes: A NAMED BUILDING WITH A PLACE ON THE GROUND, SOLD AT AUCTION. 'The Building formerly occupied as the Meeting House, opposite the bridge over the North Branch of the Chicago river' is a structure, a former use, and an anchor — and the anchor is the north branch bridge that claim c001 shows the Trustees repairing in the same issue, so the two claims fix each other. FORMERLY occupied is the point: the congregation had moved on, and the Presbyterian meeting house dedicated in January (1834-01-21, claim c002 there) is where they had moved to. So this building is standing in February 1834 and is on the market. WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED is which side of the river it stood on, how big it was, or what it was built of; the notice says none of it. The two town lots sold with it are given by lot and block and are separate property, not the building's own description.

claims.notes: THE EAGLE HOTEL, AND IT IS STEELE'S. The paper names the house twice over — the sign it trades under and the man who keeps it — and that pairing is what makes a tavern placeable later, because deeds and plats carry the keeper's name and advertisements carry the sign. It is the town's meeting room in February 1834: this notice, the county meeting of the 15th in the same column, and the auction of claim c002 are all held at it. NO ADDRESS IS GIVEN and none is supplied. The convention business is out of town and is not claimed here; what is claimed is the house.

claims.notes: A TRADE SHOP PLACED OFF A NAMED HOUSE. 'Nearly opposite the Chicago Hotel' puts a blacksmith's forge on the far side of a street from a tavern that the storefront pass can look for, and 'nearly' is the paper's own hedge and is kept. What the shop MAKES is the reconstruction's interest: prairie ploughs, manufactured on the premises, which is a working forge and not a farrier's corner. THE STREET IS NOT NAMED and is not supplied — the Chicago Hotel's own address does not appear in this issue, so the anchor is real but not yet resolved to ground; that is a placement to inherit, not a gap to fill. Standing since December 1833, so it is documented before the scene date and stands in 1835 on a survival liberty unless contradicted.

claims.notes: THE STEAM SAW MILL, AND A LEGAL DESCRIPTION OF THE GROUND IT STANDS ON. This is the rare shape: a named industrial building tied not to a street but to the public land survey — the west half of the south west quarter of section 4, township 39 north, range 14 east — which is a georeferenceable rectangle rather than a direction from a corner. A steam saw mill is also the town's own supply of sawn lumber, which is what claim c011's building-materials prices are quoting, so the mill and the lumber column in the same issue are one story. WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED: the notice describes the ground and not the mill — no dimensions, no storeys, no materials, and nothing about whether it was running. The printed year reads 1833 and is normalized to 1834: the notice is dated January 8 and is running in a February 1834 paper whose neighbours in the same column are all dated January 1834, and a January dateline a year stale would have expired the standing advertisement.

claims.notes: THE PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH IS A WORKING PUBLIC ROOM NINE DAYS AFTER IT WAS DEDICATED, and this is the corroboration T-0310's building claim asked for. The Chicago Temperance Society holds its ANNUAL meeting in it on the evening of Thursday 30 January 1834 — 'so large an assembly' — elects officers and hears an address. For the reconstruction the building is the claim: a house big enough to seat the town's respectable and intelligent citizens, in use eighteen months before the scene date. THE SLATE IS THE OTHER HALF: John T. Temple and Josiah C. Goodhue (both styled Dr.), Philo Carpenter as secretary and treasurer, Capt. D. Wilcox and Lieut. J. L. Thompson of the U.S. Army — Fort Dearborn officers sitting on a town committee, which is what the fort's relation to the town actually looked like — Dr. D. Harmon, Dr. H. Van Den Bogart, Edward W. Casey esq., Col. Rich'd J. Hamilton, Lieut. L. T. Jamison and the Revs. A. C. Freeman and one whose name the column edge cut away. Philo Carpenter is the druggist the first issue's source record names (1833-11-26); Hamilton is the county clerk who attests the estray notice on page 3 of this same issue and who married a couple in it. The column is a Tesseract fallback with its left edge shaved, so the supplies are single cut letters; every name is read off the line uncut.

claims.notes: WHAT IT COST TO BUILD IN CHICAGO IN FEBRUARY 1834, quoted weekly by a merchant. The line is worth a card because it is a LIST OF THE MATERIALS THE TOWN ACTUALLY BUILT WITH, named by the market rather than inferred from surviving buildings: assorted poplar lumber by the thousand feet, shingles, square timber sold by the running foot, lath, a perch measure, lime by the barrel, and a cord measure. Poplar heading the lumber quotation is the useful detail — the cheap local softwood, not imported pine — and square timber priced by length is the balloon frame's predecessor still being sold. THE ROW LABELS ARE PARTLY CUT AWAY by the Tesseract fallback's left margin and the two supplies marked with a question mark are exactly that: guesses at a label, flagged rather than asserted, and the numbers beside them are not read as attaching to any named material. Nothing here is upgraded to a dimension.

claims.notes: SQUARE TIMBER LYING ON A NAMED LOT IN KINZIE'S ADDITION, which is a small claim that does two useful things. It puts Hiram Pearsons on Water Lot No. 12 in Kinzie's Addition — a lot number and an addition name, which is the finest-grained land citation in this issue after the saw mill's section description — and it shows building timber stockpiled on a town lot in January, which is what a lot looks like before it is built on. The three sticks are the same 'square timber' the price current quotes by the running foot in claim c011. WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED is that Pearsons owned the lot or was building on it; the notice says the timber was his and was taken from there.

claims.notes: A LICENSED AUCTIONEER SETS UP IN CHICAGO IN JANUARY 1834, and he is the same J. Bates, jr. who is crying the sale of the old Meeting House at the Eagle Hotel two days after this paper (claim c002). A licence taken out is a dated start, which is what makes this worth a card: the trade begins here rather than being assumed to have been running. No premises are named and none is supplied — an auctioneer of the period worked wherever the goods were, which the Eagle Hotel sale demonstrates.

claims.notes: THE CHICAGO LETTER LIST, AND THIS WITNESS CARRIES IT IN BOTH ITS PRINTED COLUMNS. Under the owner's ruling 1 a listed name mints a resident candidate, so this is the month's census proxy and every name here carries `letter_list_only: true`. SEVENTY-ONE ENTRIES ARE PRINTED IN THIS COLUMN and seventy-one are extracted; seventy persons are minted, because two entries are shaved past reading by the segmenter's left margin ('avi ichson', 'William [?]ing 2') and are recorded WITHOUT being minted, while 'Lamira & Laura Carrier' is one printed entry naming two people and mints both. THE RELATION TO T-0310 IS THE POINT OF READING IT AGAIN. That pass minted 97 names from the printing of 1834-01-28 and said plainly that 97 was a FLOOR and not the printed length, because the .docx extraction crushed the list's two alphabetical columns into eight paragraph lines. This printing is a ruled .txt and keeps the two columns apart, so the floor rises: 71 entries in the left column here, plus the right column recorded in claim c017, is 147 printed entries for the same quarterly list. AND THE DATELINE DISAGREES BY TWO DAYS — this heading reads 'January 3, 1834' where T-0310 read the list as the 1 January return. The disagreement is recorded and NOT harmonized: one of the two readings is wrong and a scan will say which, and quietly picking one would destroy the only evidence that there is a question. The year is normalized from the transcription's '1934', which is the one correction here that is not a judgement — the paper is dated 4 February 1834. Names are normalized only where the letterform confusion is unambiguous; where it is a guess ('Cyitha', 'Aaron Demis', 'Nathan Huchine', 'Anthony Becra') the printed form stands. 'A. O. T. Breed' is the one entry corroborated inside this issue: he advertises his own winding-up on page 3 (claim c008), which is what a name confirmed by a second kind of claim looks like.

claims.notes: THE OTHER HALF OF THE SAME LIST, RECORDED IN FULL AND MINTED NOT AT ALL — and the refusal to mint is the claim. Seventy-six surname fragments are printed in this column and seventy-six are extracted, which with claim c016's seventy-one is 147 entries for the whole printing. NOT ONE is turned into a person, because the segmenter cut the column between the given name and the surname: the given names are at the shaved right edge of the previous column and the surnames at the shaved left edge of this one, and the two runs are of different lengths, so pairing them would be a fabrication with a plausible shape. The gazetteer is keyed on the WHOLE normalized name for exactly this reason — 'Cohen, P.' and 'Cohen, J.' are two people — so a bare surname would mint somebody who is not anybody. What this column IS good for is a count and a reading of the list's length, and for names that recur elsewhere: 'Kercheval', 'Scarritt' (the Rev. Mr. Scarritt marries a couple on the Dupage in this issue, claim c012), 'Temple' twice (Dr. John T. Temple presides over the Temperance Society in this issue, claim c009) and 'B. Winn & Co.' are all read here without being claimed as those people. Readings marked with a question mark are guesses at a cut word and are flagged rather than asserted; the rest stand as printed. A FULLER WITNESS WOULD SETTLE IT: the page images of PDF page 4 of Jan1834-Mar1834.pdf carry the column whole, and a scan-verified pass over them would mint this half and raise T-0310's floor properly.

claims.notes: A SHOEMAKER'S SHOP PLACED NEXT DOOR TO A STOREFRONT THE PROJECT ALREADY HAS. 'Next door to P. Cohen's Store' is the tightest kind of relative placement — one door, not 'near' or 'a few doors below' — and Peter Cohen's store at the east end of South Water Street is the T-0257 fixture's own business, carried from the scene-date issue of 1835-07-01. So this puts L. W. Montgomery's boot and shoe shop on South Water Street next to a door already placed, eighteen months before the scene date. THE SIDE IS NOT STATED — 'next door' does not say east or west — and it is not supplied. Standing since December 1833, so it stands in the 1835 town on a survival liberty unless contradicted. The proprietor's surname is cut at 'MONT' and completed from the identical advertisement in the following issue (1834-02-11, page 4 column 3, 'L. W. MONTGOMERY'), which is a supply from a second witness rather than a guess.

claims.notes: TWO BUILDINGS STANDING EMPTY AND ADVERTISED TO LET, which is the plainest kind of evidence that they exist. The count is the claim — TWO — and John Wright is the man to enquire of; the same advertisement runs the following week as 'Dwellings to Let, from the first day of June 1834' over the same name (1834-02-11, claim c008 there), which is what supplies the term here and also says what kind of buildings they are. NO STREET, NO SIZE, NO MATERIAL, and none is supplied. The heading is cut at 't' and completed from that second witness. This is also the third to-let notice the epic has found in the Democrat's first year and it is worth the card for that alone: the town's building stock was ahead of its tenants in the winter of 1833-34.

claims.notes: A COUNTED OFFSET FROM A NAMED CORNER, WHICH IS THE BEST PLACEMENT SHAPE THE PAPERS GIVE. 'Second door west from the corner of Franklin and South Water streets' names an intersection AND a distance along it AND a direction — enough to put a door on a specific lot frontage once the block is dealt, which is more than almost any other advertisement in this month manages. It also fixes a second intersection on South Water Street beside the LaSalle corner (P. F. Peck, 1834-02-11 claim c004) and the Clark corner the Democrat itself prints from, so the street's documented anchors are accumulating westward. The advertiser's surname is cut at 'SPRI' and the same notice runs the following week equally cut ('[Step]hen G. …, Counsellor at Law … [second] door west from the corner [of Franklin and] South Water-streets', 1834-02-11 page 4 column 4), so the two witnesses supply each other's halves; the reading 'G. Spring' is marked as the cut form it is and is not asserted beyond it.

claims.notes: A BAKERY AND DRINKING HOUSE CALLED THE MAN TRAP, PLACED OFF R. A. KINZIE'S STORE. Three things worth having. The SIGN is a joke the town would have known — 'their Man Trap' — and named premises are how a walkable scene gets signboards that are not invented. The PLACEMENT is relative to Mr. R. A. Kinzie's Store, which is a fixed point the same month advertises twice more (1834-02-18 and 1834-02-25, R. A. Kinzie selling white fish, whiskey and flour). And the TRADE is bread, cakes, pastry and liquors of every description from one counter, which is what a frontier bakery actually was. HOW MANY DOORS, and on which side, is cut away by the column edge and is NOT supplied — 'one [door … ] of' is where the reading stops. The address to 'Hoosiers, Wolverines and Suckers' and to 'our old patrons, the Pottawatamies' is the advertisement's own voice and is quoted, not smoothed: it records who the shop expected through its door in the winter after the 1833 treaty.
